name: Half Guard Wrestle-Up
keyCorrections: If they flatten you during the wrestle-up: you lost the underhook — re-pummel before trying again
If you cannot find the single leg: they posted the leg back — switch to the front headlock using the underhook
If they guillotine you: your head was too high — keep your forehead to their jaw as you stand
description: Turn half guard from defense into a single leg when you win the underhook or hip angle. The wrestle-up is the highest-value offensive transition from half guard — it converts a defensive position into a takedown opportunity.
shortInstruction: Win the underhook, create a hip angle, post on your outside foot, and drive to a single leg. If they resist the single leg, come up to a front headlock.
summary: The half guard wrestle-up transforms half guard from a defensive pin into an offensive takedown entry. The sequence is: win the underhook → turn to face them → post your outside foot → drive to a single leg. The wrestle-up works because it catches the opponent in the transition between passing and pinning — they are not fully committed to either, making them vulnerable to the sudden stand-up.
whyItWorks: The underhook gives you upper body control — they cannot crossface or flatten you as you stand
Creating a hip angle (turning to face them) aligns your body for the stand-up — you drive forward, not sideways
The single leg entry from half guard is unexpected — most opponents expect a sweep, not a takedown
A failed wrestle-up often resets to neutral rather than leaving you in a worse position
commonMistakes: Trying to wrestle up without the underhook — they will crossface you and flatten you back down
Standing up straight instead of staying low — a tall posture exposes the single leg counter and gives up the underhook
Not creating enough separation before standing — you need 6-8 inches of space to post the foot
Giving up on the wrestle-up too early — commit to the stand-up or you will be stuck in between
coachingCues: Create the angle, post the foot
Stay low, drive to the leg
safetySummary: Do not stand up with a straight back — this exposes your neck to guillotines and your back to takedowns
If the opponent sprawls on the wrestle-up, drop back to guard rather than fighting the sprawl
Be careful of knee strain when posting from half guard — the outside foot must be planted firmly

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The half guard wrestle-up has four phases: Underhook → Hip Angle → Stand → Single Leg

decisionTree.action: win the underhook and control their posture. Your head should be on their chest (forehead to sternum)
hip escape to create 6-8 inches of space. Turn your hips to face them at a 45-degree angle
post your outside foot and drive to a standing position. Stay low — your head should not rise above their shoulder
as you stand, attack their far leg for a single leg. If they block, drive into their hips for a body lock
transition to the front headlock using your underhook grip to snap them down

moneyDetails: The half guard wrestle-up is the highest-value transition from half guard — it scores 2 takedown points and lands you on top
Mastering the wrestle-up gives you a third option from half guard (sweep, submission, or wrestle-up)
The wrestle-up is particularly effective against pressure passers who commit weight forward
fixItFast: If they pressure forward: use their momentum — wrestle-up into the direction they are pushing
If they back away: stand up fully and re-engage from a neutral position
If they switch to a knee cut pass: re-pummel the underhook and hip escape to create space
